description: Limits the search to one pod or log collection boundary so results stay relevant to the environment you are investigating.
Identifies which parser or source type produced the event, such as access logs, app logs, or async orchestration logs.
Buckets events into fixed time windows so you can trend counts or averages over time.
Builds multiple derived calculations side by side so one query can return several related metrics.
Aggregates raw events into summary values such as counts, averages, maximums, or grouped totals.
Counts matching events. It is the first thing to look at when you want throughput or error volume.
Counts unique values, which is useful for sessions, ECIDs, users, or hosts.
Computes the average of a numeric field such as Duration or ProcessingDuration.
Finds the highest observed value in the result set, useful for spotting spikes.
Collects matching values into one grouped result row so you can keep important identifiers such as victim session IDs.
Matches a partial string pattern. Use it when the full URI or message varies but still follows a known prefix.
Chooses which columns to keep in the output so you can reduce noise and focus on the data that matters.
Orders the results so the most important rows appear first, such as highest latency or highest volume.
Keeps only the top portion of the sorted output, usually the most important rows to review first.
Execution context identifier used to tie together multiple log events from the same business flow.
A response time style field. High averages indicate broad slowness and high max values indicate spikes.
A processing time field often used for async or orchestration stages.
The session holding a lock or resource that is preventing other sessions from moving forward.
The response status code or status indicator. It is often the fastest way to separate successes from failures.
The request path. Grouping or filtering by URI helps isolate one API or endpoint family.
